Dataset Name: cleaned_gene_expression.csv
Dataset Description: source: UCSC Xena - TOIL RSEM FPKM
normalization: RSEM expected_count, then log2(fpkm+0.001) transformed
platform: Illumina HiSeq RNA-Seq
data_type: Gene expression quantification
url: https://toil.xenahubs.net/download/tcga_RSEM_gene_fpkm.gz
dimensions:

  samples: 470
description: Rows are genes (Ensembl gene IDs), columns are samples (TCGA barcodes)

  clinical_patients: 470
  matched_samples: 470
  note: Samples filtered to match patients in cleaned_clinical_data.csv
data_description:
  values: Log2(FPKM + 0.001) - normalized gene expression levels
  interpretation: Higher values indicate higher gene expression. Values are continuous and log-transformed.
  missing_data: Genes with all zeros or NaN across samples were removed

- Gene identifiers are in the index (first column)
- Sample identifiers are in the column headers (TCGA barcodes)
- Data is pre-normalized and log-transformed, ready for analysis

PREVIOUS EXPLORATION:

Hypothesis: Patients with elevated lactate dehydrogenase activity—as approximated by high LDHA gene expression—exhibit higher tumor proliferation (mitotic count) and a distinct proliferation‐related gene expression signature compared to patients with low LDHA expression.

Experiment objective: Because clinical LDH annotations are too sparse, use LDHA gene expression as a continuous proxy for LDH activity. Test whether high LDHA expression correlates with increased mitotic counts and distinct differential expression of proliferation genes.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv and cleaned_gene_expression.csv (genes × samples); ensure sample barcodes match first 12 characters to clinical bcr_patient_barcode.  
2. From gene expression data, extract the row corresponding to LDHA (HUGO symbol: “LDHA”) and compute its expression per sample.  
3. Map each sample’s LDHA expression to its patient record; merge with clinical data.  
4. Filter to patients with non‐missing mitotic_count_per_mm2 and age_at_diagnosis and gender.  
5. Dichotomize patients into “High‐LDHA” vs “Low‐LDHA” groups around the median LDHA expression.  
6. Compare mitotic_count_per_mm2 between High vs Low LDHA groups using an appropriate two‐sample test (t‐test or Wilcoxon).  
7. Build a linear model (e.g., OLS) or use limma to identify genes differentially expressed between High‐LDHA vs Low‐LDHA, adjusting for age_at_diagnosis and gender. Apply FDR correction and extract genes with FDR<0.05.  
8. From a curated proliferation gene set (e.g., Hallmark E2F targets), test for enrichment among genes upregulated in the High‐LDHA group via Fisher’s exact test or preranked GSEA.  
9. Visualize results: volcano plot for DE genes and a bar or dot plot of enrichment statistics.

Deliverables:
• Table of patient counts, group means, test statistics, and p‐value for mitotic count comparison.  
• Data frame of DE results: gene, logFC, p‐value, FDR.  
• Volcano plot of differential expression (highlighting FDR<0.05).  
• Enrichment analysis report: overlap counts, odds ratio, p‐value for proliferation gene set.  
• Brief summary PDF or notebook section interpreting whether high LDHA expression is associated with increased mitotic count and proliferation signature.

Analysis:
The analysis completed successfully with 170 samples (85 High‐LDHA, 85 Low‐LDHA):

• Mitotic count comparison (High vs Low LDHA): t = 0.412, p = 0.681 → no significant difference.  
• Differential expression (OLS adjusting for age and gender): 17,519 genes at FDR < 0.05.  
• Top 10 DE genes (sorted by FDR):
  – ENSG00000134333.13: logFC=+1.26, FDR=5.96e-33
  – ENSG00000166788.9: logFC=+0.69, FDR=9.61e-08
  – ENSG00000181444.12: logFC=–1.25, FDR=1.02e-07
  – …

Volcano plot shows many significant genes (red) at both positive and negative log‐fold changes. Enrichment for E2F targets was not performed (requires gene set library).

Review:
The revised experiment substituted LDHA expression for sparse clinical LDH measurements, following the updated plan. It successfully dichotomized 170 patients into High/Low LDHA groups, performed a t-test on mitotic counts (no significant difference: p=0.681), and conducted gene-wise OLS (adjusting for age and gender) identifying 17,519 DE genes at FDR<0.05. A volcano plot was generated. Enrichment analysis was omitted due to library availability but the gene set and method were defined. Overall, the implementation follows the revised plan and tests the hypothesis.

content:
PREVIOUS EXPLORATION:

Hypothesis: Patient age at diagnosis is inversely correlated with expression of a proliferation gene signature (e.g., MKI67, PCNA, MCM family).

Experiment objective: Compute a proliferation score per sample and test its correlation with age.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Define a proliferation signature gene list: MKI67, PCNA, MCM2–MCM7.  
2. Map each symbol to its Ensembl ID via mygene and extract expression rows.  
3. For each sample, compute the mean expression across these genes as the proliferation score.  
4. Merge proliferation scores with age_at_diagnosis.  
5. Plot scatter of proliferation score vs age; compute Spearman correlation and p‐value.  
6. Divide patients into age quartiles and compare proliferation score across quartiles via Kruskal–Wallis test.

Deliverables:
• Proliferation score per sample.  
• Scatter plot with Spearman ρ and p‐value.  
• Kruskal–Wallis statistic and p‐value across age quartiles.  
• Boxplot of proliferation score by age quartile.

Analysis:
The proliferation score was successfully computed for 462 patients (mean ≈5.03, SD ≈0.60). Spearman correlation between age at diagnosis and proliferation score was effectively zero (ρ=–0.002, p=0.966), indicating no monotonic relationship. Comparing proliferation scores across age quartiles via Kruskal–Wallis yielded H=7.134 (p=0.0678), also non‐significant. Overall, there is no evidence that proliferation signature expression is inversely correlated with age in this cohort.

Review:
Hypothesis: Patient age at diagnosis is inversely correlated with expression of a proliferation gene signature (MKI67, PCNA, MCM2–MCM7).

Implementation followed the plan: proliferative gene symbols were mapped to Ensembl IDs, expression values were extracted, and a proliferation score (mean expression) was computed for each of 462 samples with available age data. Spearman correlation between age_at_diagnosis and proliferation score was effectively zero (rho = –0.002, p = 0.966), indicating no monotonic relationship. When dividing patients into age quartiles, the Kruskal–Wallis test yielded H = 7.134 (p = 0.0678), also non‐significant.

Conclusion: There is no evidence supporting an inverse correlation between patient age and the proliferation signature in this cohort.

Hypothesis: Patients with high tumor mutational burden exhibit elevated expression of immune checkpoint genes (e.g., PDCD1, CD274, CTLA4, LAG3, TIGIT).

Experiment objective: Assess whether tumor mutational burden (TMB) per patient correlates with expression of immune checkpoint genes.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv, cleaned_gene_expression.csv, and cleaned_mutations.csv.
2. From cleaned_mutations.csv, count total somatic mutations per patient_id to define TMB.
3. Match each gene expression sample to its patient via the first 12 characters of the sample barcode.
4. Define an immune checkpoint gene list: PDCD1, CD274, CTLA4, LAG3, TIGIT.
5. Map each symbol to Ensembl IDs and extract corresponding rows from the gene expression matrix.
6. Compute an immune checkpoint score per sample as the mean log₂(FPKM+0.001) across these genes.
7. Merge per‐patient TMB with the immune checkpoint score.
8. Test the Spearman correlation between TMB and immune checkpoint score.
9. Dichotomize patients into High‐TMB vs Low‐TMB around the median and compare immune scores using a Wilcoxon rank‐sum test.
10. Visualize results with (a) a scatter plot of TMB vs immune score (including regression line and Spearman ρ), and (b) a boxplot comparing High vs Low TMB groups.

Deliverables:
• Table of patients with TMB, immune checkpoint scores, Spearman ρ, and p‐value.
• Results of Wilcoxon test comparing immune scores in High vs Low TMB groups (test statistic and p‐value).
• Scatter plot of TMB vs immune score with annotation of Spearman correlation.
• Boxplot of immune score by TMB group.
• Brief narrative interpreting whether higher TMB associates with elevated checkpoint expression.

{"code":"import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import spearmanr, mannwhitneyu
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Load data
clinical = pd.read_csv('cleaned_clinical_data.csv', usecols=['bcr_patient_barcode'])
expr = pd.read_csv('cleaned_gene_expression.csv', index_col=0)
mut = pd.read_csv('cleaned_mutations.csv')

# 2. Compute TMB (mutations per patient)
tmb = mut.groupby('patient_id').size().rename('TMB').reset_index()
# include patients with zero mutations
all_patients = pd.DataFrame({'patient_id': clinical['bcr_patient_barcode'].unique()})
tmb = all_patients.merge(tmb, on='patient_id', how='left').fillna(0)

# 3. Map samples to patients for expression
samples = expr.columns.tolist()
patient_ids = [s[:12] for s in samples]

# 4. Immune checkpoint genes and mapping to Ensembl IDs
genes = ['PDCD1', 'CD274', 'CTLA4', 'LAG3', 'TIGIT']
try:
    import mygene
except ImportError:
    import subprocess, sys
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, '-m', 'pip', 'install', '--quiet', 'mygene'])
    import mygene
mg = mygene.MyGeneInfo()
res = mg.querymany(genes, scopes='symbol', fields='ensembl.gene', species='human')
# extract Ensembl IDs
ensembl_ids = []
for r in res:
    gene_info = r.get('ensembl')
    if isinstance(gene_info, list):
        en = gene_info[0].get('gene')
    elif isinstance(gene_info, dict):
        en = gene_info.get('gene')
    else:
        en = None
    if en:
        # match prefix ignoring version
        if en not in ensembl_ids:
            ensembl_ids.append(en)

# 5. Extract expression rows for these genes
mask = expr.index.to_series().apply(lambda x: any(x.startswith(e) for e in ensembl_ids))
imm_expr = expr[mask]

# 6. Compute immune checkpoint score per sample (mean expression)
immune_scores = imm_expr.mean(axis=0)
immune_df = pd.DataFrame({'sample': immune_scores.index, 'immune_score': immune_scores.values})
immune_df['patient_id'] = immune_df['sample'].str[:12]

# 7. Merge TMB with immune scores per patient
df = tmb.merge(immune_df.groupby('patient_id')['immune_score'].mean().reset_index(), on='patient_id', how='inner')

# 8. Spearman correlation
rho, p_spearman = spearmanr(df['TMB'], df['immune_score'])

# 9. Dichotomize by median TMB and Wilcoxon test
median_tmb = df['TMB'].median()
df['TMB_group'] = np.where(df['TMB'] >= median_tmb, 'High', 'Low')
g1 = df.loc[df['TMB_group']=='High', 'immune_score']
g2 = df.loc[df['TMB_group']=='Low', 'immune_score']
stat_w, p_w = mannwhitneyu(g1, g2, alternative='two-sided')

# 10. Outputs
print(f"Number of patients with both TMB and immune scores: {len(df)}")
print(f"Spearman correlation: rho = {rho:.3f}, p-value = {p_spearman:.3g}")
print(f"Wilcoxon rank-sum test (High vs Low TMB): statistic = {stat_w:.3f}, p-value = {p_w:.3g}")
print("\nSample of patient-level results:")
print(df[['patient_id','TMB','immune_score','TMB_group']].head(), "\n")

# 11. Visualizations
plt.figure(figsize=(6,5))
plt.scatter(df['TMB'], df['immune_score'], alpha=0.7)
# regression line
a = np.polyfit(df['TMB'], df['immune_score'], 1)
plt.plot(df['TMB'], np.polyval(a, df['TMB']), color='red', lw=1)
plt.xlabel('Tumor Mutational Burden')
plt.ylabel('Immune Checkpoint Score')
plt.title(f'Scatter: TMB vs Immune Score\nSpearman rho={rho:.2f}, p={p_spearman:.3g}')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

plt.figure(figsize=(6,5))
import seaborn as sns
sns.boxplot(x='TMB_group', y='immune_score', data=df, palette='Set2')
plt.xlabel('TMB Group')
plt.ylabel('Immune Checkpoint Score')
plt.title('Immune Score by TMB Group\nWilcoxon p=' + f"{p_w:.3g}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()"}
